# Baselines, datasets and the fair-comparison protocol {#sec-baselines}

**ISLA is measured against the two public slice-attention transformers
with the strongest record on industrial aerodynamics, GeoTransolver and
Transolver, on three datasets, under one protocol that fixes everything
except the architecture.** The baselines are strong, not straw:
GeoTransolver has at least as many parameters as ISLA and receives raw
coordinates that ISLA never sees; both run at their own best learning rate;
neither is ever modified. This chapter says what each baseline computes and
sees, states one rule about how a problem's global conditions enter any
model, lists the protocol as nine rules, introduces the datasets (their
details are in @sec-datasets-detail), and closes with the protocol table
every cross-architecture number in the book is produced under.

```{python}
#| label: setup-baselines
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm
from matplotlib.collections import LineCollection
PF = RES / "problem_figures_2026-09-22"

def load_problem(name):
    """One representative sample of a dataset, reduced for plotting (results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/)."""
    z = np.load(PF / f"{name}.npz"); meta = json.load(open(PF / f"{name}.json"))
    return {k: z[k] for k in z.files}, meta

def bc_segments(ax, pts, cells, kinds, lw=4.0, zorder=3):
    """Draw line cells colored by boundary-condition kind (keys of palette.BC)."""
    segs = pts[cells][:, :, :2]
    ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs, colors=[BC[k] for k in kinds], linewidths=lw, capstyle="butt", zorder=zorder))

def field_scatter(ax, xy, v, s=3.0, signed=False, vmin=None, vmax=None):
    if signed:
        lim = max(abs(np.nanmin(v)), abs(np.nanmax(v))) if vmin is None else None
        norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0.0, vmin=(-lim if vmin is None else vmin), vmax=(lim if vmax is None else vmax))
        return ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], c=v, s=s, lw=0, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm, rasterized=True)
    return ax.scatter(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], c=v, s=s, lw=0, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=vmin, vmax=vmax, rasterized=True)

def small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, label, **kw):
    cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, fraction=0.035, pad=0.02, **kw); cb.outline.set_visible(False); cb.ax.tick_params(labelsize=8)
    cb.set_label(label, fontsize=8.5)
    return cb

def bc_legend(ax, kinds, loc="lower right", extra=()):
    from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
    handles = [Line2D([], [], color=BC[k], lw=4, label=BC_LABEL[k]) for k in kinds] + list(extra)
    ax.legend(handles=handles, loc=loc, fontsize=8, frameon=True, facecolor="white", edgecolor=BASELINE)
```

## The baselines and what each one sees {#sec-part-baseline}

**GeoTransolver and Transolver share ISLA's routing mechanism and differ in
what they are allowed to see: raw coordinates in a frame, and the problem's
global vector as a raw feature.** Transolver (Wu et al., ICML 2024, arXiv
[2402.02366](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.02366)) is a transformer for physics
fields on unstructured point sets. Each layer assigns every point a softmax
mixture over a fixed number of *slices*, pools point features into one token
per slice, runs attention among the slice tokens, and scatters the result
back through the same mixture: *physics attention*. GeoTransolver adds a
geometry encoder and a global-context projector. @fig-family-diagram places
ISLA beside them.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-family-diagram
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   What each architecture is handed, and where they differ. Gray boxes
%%|   are data; the routing mechanism (solid blue) is shared by the whole
%%|   family. GeoTransolver and Transolver receive coordinates in the
%%|   dataset's frame and the global vector as a vector; ISLA receives only
%%|   invariants of the same inputs and its slices carry the surface measure
%%|   (dashed blue: fixed maps with no parameters). How to read this: the
%%|   diagram shows inputs and structure, not accuracy; the learned blocks are
%%|   the same kind of object in all three.
flowchart LR
    classDef data fill:#f4f3ee,stroke:#898781,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef learned fill:#e6f0fb,stroke:#2a78d6,color:#0b0b0b
    classDef fixed fill:#ffffff,stroke:#2a78d6,stroke-dasharray:4 3,color:#0b0b0b

    subgraph B["GeoTransolver / Transolver"]
        direction TB
        B1["per point: centered coordinates, unit normal<br/>global: the far-field vector (a unit direction under the protocol)"]:::data
        B2["GeoTransolver only: geometry encoder,<br/>global-context projector"]:::learned
        B3["physics attention × layers:<br/>softmax routing of points into slices,<br/>attention among slices, scatter back"]:::learned
        B4["linear head: pressure, wall shear"]:::learned
        B1 --> B2 --> B3 --> B4
    end
    subgraph I["ISLA"]
        direction TB
        I1["per point: position, unit normal, measure weight<br/>global: unit direction(s), scalars"]:::data
        I2["invariant seed; length unit = RMS pairwise distance"]:::fixed
        I3["slice layers × 12:<br/>measure-weighted routing, anchors,<br/>relational invariants, read-back"]:::learned
        I4["linear head on invariants → equivariant basis"]:::fixed
        I1 --> I2 --> I3 --> I4
    end
```

**GeoTransolver** is the recipe's default surface model. Per surface point
it receives the coordinates, centered on the case, and the unit normal as a
six-channel feature; the far-field vector is a three-channel global feature.
Its *geometry encoder* takes the coordinates a second time through a
dedicated embedding path that conditions the slice attention; the
ball-query local-feature path is off throughout this program, because it is
off in the recipe's shipped configuration; the GeoTransolver compared here
is therefore the one a user gets by running the recipe unmodified, not the
strongest configuration the class can express. It is not rotation- or
translation-equivariant: rotate the car and it sees a different input
(@sec-pose).

::: {#sec-transolver}
**Transolver** is the same family without the geometry encoder, the control
that isolates what the encoder contributes. Per point it receives coordinates
and normal; the far-field vector is broadcast to every point.
:::

**ISLA** receives position, unit normal and measure weight per point and
each global direction as a unit vector, consumed only through invariants
and equivariant anchors (@sec-isla). @tbl-architectures gives the three
configurations side by side; the parameter counts and training footprints
are in @tbl-isla-cost. On the interior tasks the baseline is
GeoTransolver-volume, the recipe's volume configuration of the same class,
described with those tasks in @sec-interior.

| architecture | per-point inputs | global input | layers | hidden | slices |
|---|---|---|--:|--:|--:|
| GeoTransolver | centered coordinates, unit normal; coordinates again through the geometry encoder | the far-field vector through the global-context projector: a unit direction under the protocol | 12 | 256 | 256 |
| Transolver | centered coordinates, unit normal | the far-field vector, broadcast per point: a unit direction under the protocol | 8 | 256 | 256 |
| ISLA | position, unit normal, measure weight, through invariants and anchors only | unit direction(s) and global scalars | 12 | see @sec-using-config | 256 |

: The three architectures compared on the aerodynamic datasets. *Per-point
inputs*: channels attached to each of the 200,000 sampled surface cells per
case under the reporting protocol. *Layers*: soft-slice attention blocks.
*Hidden*: width of the per-point feature. How to read this: the table
states what each model is handed, not how accurate it is or what it costs
(@sec-using-cost). Configuration source:
`unified_external_aero_recipe/conf/model/{isla_surface,geotransolver_surface,transolver_surface}.yaml`.
{#tbl-architectures}

### Global directions enter as unit vectors, magnitudes as scalars {#sec-unit-direction-rule}

**A problem's global conditions enter every architecture in one form:
directions as unit vectors, magnitudes as scalars.** The rule is a property
of the problem, not of any dataset's units. A direction carries no scale;
whatever scale the pipeline attaches to it (the units the solver ran in) is
an accident of the dataset that a model would have to learn to ignore. A
magnitude that matters physically, a far-field speed or a Reynolds number,
is a separate scalar with its own place in the input. ISLA enforces the
rule by construction: it normalizes its global vectors and takes magnitudes
only through rank-0 `global_inputs` (@sec-isla-inputs). GeoTransolver and
Transolver consume whatever vector the pipeline hands them, so for them the
rule is a protocol requirement, and every dataset pipeline of the recipe
writes the far-field direction as a unit vector.

The motivating control is visible before training. GeoTransolver's
global-context projector applies linear maps and a slice softmax to the
vector directly, so its conditioning depends on the magnitude. At unit
magnitude a head of the untrained projector spreads over most of the 256
slices; at the magnitude of the HiLiftAeroML solver's velocity (in inches
per second) it routes almost all of its weight to one (@tbl-projector).
Transolver concatenates the raw vector into every point's features, with
the same hazard in a different place. Training can in principle rescale
either path, so these numbers are the initialization signature; the trained
measurement, in the collapsed note below, is what the rule rests on.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-projector
#| output: asis
cond = J("geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json")["results"]
out = "| magnitude of the global vector | occupied slices per head (entropy-equivalent, min to max over heads) | largest context entry |\n|---:|---|---:|\n"
labels = {1.0: "1 (unit direction)", 38.9: "38.9 (DrivAerML's velocity, m/s)", 2679.5054741899685: "2,679.5 (HiLiftAeroML's velocity, in/s)"}
for r in cond:
    lab = next(v for k, v in labels.items() if abs(k - r["drive_magnitude"]) < 1e-6)
    out += f"| {lab} | {r['effective_slices_min']:.1f} to {r['effective_slices_max']:.1f} of 256 | {r['context_abs_max']:.2f} |\n"
print(out)
print(": Conditioning of GeoTransolver's global-context projector at initialization against the magnitude of the "
      "global vector it receives, at the recipe's projector dimensions with untrained weights. "
      "How to read this: a head that occupies one slice has lost its ability to condition on the direction; "
      "this is a property of the untrained network, and the trained consequence is in the note below. "
      "Data: results/geotransolver_drive_conditioning_2026-09-08.json. {#tbl-projector}")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="The trained consequence, at the exploration budget"}
At 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases with the same cases, seeds and budget in
both arms, GeoTransolver and Transolver fed the unit direction are each more
accurate than their physical-velocity twin on every one of the 180
validation cases, by a median factor above three (@tbl-unit-vs-physical).
The table is a control on an input scale, measured at the exploration
budget of 10,000 cells; it makes no accuracy claim about any architecture
and appears nowhere else in the book.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-unit-vs-physical
#| output: asis
fp35 = J("fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json")["runs"]
ud = J("udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json")["paired"]
fp = lambda keys: [fp35[k]["fields"]["pressure_l2"]["fp32_mean"] for k in keys]
arms = [
    ("GeoTransolver, physical velocity, lr 1e-3", fp([f"lad_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 1e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("GeoTransolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3 (its best at this rung)", fp([f"udrv_hl_gt_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43)])),
    ("Transolver, physical velocity, lr 3e-3", fp([f"t1_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
    ("Transolver, unit direction, lr 3e-3", fp([f"udrv_hl_transolver_super_scarce_lr3e3_seed{s}" for s in (42, 43, 44)])),
]
out = "| arm | surface pressure error, seed mean (seeds) |\n|---|---|\n"
for lab, v in arms:
    out += f"| {lab} | {mean(v):.4f} ({' / '.join(f'{x:.4f}' for x in v)}) |\n"
print(out)
g, t = ud["gt_physical_35_vs_gt_unit_35"], ud["transolver_physical_35_vs_transolver_unit_35"]
print(f": The input-scale control at 35 HiLiftAeroML training cases: area-weighted relative L2 of surface pressure "
      f"on the 180 shared validation cases, float32, final-epoch checkpoints, 10,000 cells (the exploration budget), 500 epochs. Paired per case, "
      f"the unit-direction GeoTransolver is lower than its physical-velocity twin on {g['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of "
      f"{g['n_cases']} cases (median factor {g['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}) and the unit-direction Transolver on "
      f"{t['cases_where_second_is_lower']} of {t['n_cases']} (median factor {t['median_ratio_first_over_second']:.1f}). "
      f"How to read this: the physical-velocity rows measure an input scale, not an architecture; the unit-direction rows are the protocol. Data: "
      f"results/fp32_reeval/fp32_shift_35_2026-09-09.json, results/udrv_reduction_2026-09-09.json (paired counts). {{#tbl-unit-vs-physical}}")
```
:::

Three consequences follow. Every architecture receives each global
direction as a unit vector and each magnitude as a scalar, and a comparison
against a baseline fed a raw vector is reported only as a measurement of the
input scale. The unit-direction baseline is the reference baseline on every
rung. And the input scale is fixed by rule rather than by control:
learning-rate, training-length and seed controls vary the optimizer and
cannot detect an input-scale defect. On DrivAerML, whose solver velocity is
of order tens of metres per second, and on the DrivAerML Volume task, the
trained difference between the two inputs is inside seed spread
(@sec-nb-udrv-int-verdict); the rule applies on every dataset regardless,
because a rule that depends on the dataset's units is not a rule.

## The fair-comparison protocol {#sec-fair-comparison}

**Every cross-architecture number in this book is produced under the
following rules; a comparison that violates one is not reported.** The
datasets are in @sec-datasets and their splits in @sec-splits, the metric
in @sec-metrics and the training recipe in @sec-protocol.

1. **Matched cells per case: 200,000 sampled surface cells for every
   architecture, the reporting protocol.** Accuracy is flat in the cell
   count above 100,000 for every model and is not below it
   (@sec-equal-budget), so a cell mismatch would be a handicap
   disguised as an architecture difference. A number at any other count
   carries its label.
2. **Matched epochs: 500 for every arm.** Doubling GeoTransolver's budget at
   the small rungs does not lower its error (@sec-data-efficiency), and at
   435 cars and 200,000 cells 1,000 epochs move neither ISLA nor
   GeoTransolver outside seed spread (@sec-nb-isocost-verdict), so 500
   under-trains neither.
3. **Each architecture at its own best learning rate, chosen by
   validation.** ISLA runs at 1e-3 at width 192 and at the width rule's
   rate above it (@sec-using-lr). GeoTransolver receives a two-rate control,
   1e-3 and 3e-3, on every rung and is reported at the better, a search
   that favors the baseline: at the reporting protocol its better rate is
   3e-3 on every DrivAerML rung and on the wings (@sec-lr-protocol).
4. **Every architecture receives each global direction as a unit vector and
   each magnitude as a scalar** (@sec-unit-direction-rule).
5. **Two or more seeds per cell, reported individually**, so the reader can
   see whether a ratio exceeds the seed spread.
6. **Shared validation cases**, sampled with the same seed, for every
   architecture.
7. **Paired per-case statistics where a ratio is claimed**: the count of
   validation cases on which one architecture is more accurate, with median
   and worst-decile per-case ratios, alongside the ratio of means.
8. **Sealed test splits evaluated once**, taken verbatim from the dataset
   manifest; sealed per checkpoint, not per program (@sec-splits).
9. **Preregistered bars**: each experiment states, in readout units and
   before it runs, the value that confirms and the value that refutes.

### One instrument per dataset {#sec-review-instrument}

**Every number in a family of comparisons is read from one fixed
instrument, and a control that changes the instrument is reported as a
control.** The *instrument* for a dataset is its fixed validation set and
evaluation configuration: on the DrivAerML Surface task, surface pressure
and wall shear on 48 held-out cars at 200,000 sampled cells, scored in
float32; on the DrivAerML Volume task, pressure, velocity and turbulent
viscosity at the interior queries of the same 48 cars; on HiLiftAeroML,
pressure, velocity and wall shear on 180 held-out cases shared by every
training split, at the same count and precision; on AirfRANS, pressure,
velocity and turbulent viscosity at the interior queries of its 200 test
airfoils. An instrument is never widened after a result is read from it; a
control that changes it (another cell count, a rotated pose, a biased
sampling density) is reported as such and never mixed into an in-family
number. Its limits bind where stated: 48 cars is a small validation set and
two seeds a thin noise estimate (@sec-limits).

## Resource matching {#sec-resource-matching}

**Every cross-architecture comparison states, on both sides, the parameter
count, the cells per case and the training memory, or says in the same
sentence where they differ and whether the difference could buy accuracy.**
The 435-car row of the DrivAerML Surface task is stated twice for this
reason, against GeoTransolver at its recipe width (which ISLA leads by 7%
in 0.7x the memory at 1.25x the parameters) and against the
parameter-matched GeoTransolver-512 (parity at 1.9x ISLA's memory), both
at the same cells per case; the footprints of both sides are read from
the reference cost sweep in @sec-cost-sweep. Memory is not a controlled
variable in any comparison and no accuracy result depends on it: the
checkpoints in this book are trained by implementations of the same
function that differ only in footprint. Where the two architectures are
compared at unequal parameters or memory, the section that does so says
which side has more and whether it bought accuracy (@sec-equal-budget).

### Configuration of the evidence lanes {#sec-evidence-lane-config}

**Every standing in the book is the reference configuration's
(@sec-using-config: 384 wide, 12 layers, cosine routing, the fused
geometry kernel, 5e-4) wherever its lane has been scored; the rows that
still carry the earlier protocol's ISLA (192 wide, linear routing, 1e-3)
are labeled "earlier protocol" in their table or caption and are
re-measured by the re-run of @sec-program-status.** This paragraph is the
one place the book explains the label; individual tables and captions
carry it and do not narrate the difference. The standings under the
reference configuration are the DrivAerML Surface ladder and its 435-car
row, the 35-wing rung of HiLiftAeroML, the DrivAerML Volume and AirfRANS
interior tasks, the sampling-consistency and territory probes, and every
solid and fixed-mesh dataset; the earlier protocol's lanes remain on the
210-wing, geometry and fixed-angle rungs of HiLiftAeroML, the pose and
training-law studies, the AirfRANS extrapolation splits and the
capacity, scaling and cost-frontier studies at 100,000 cells (which are
studies of deviations by design).

## Learning rate {#sec-lr-protocol}

**Each architecture trains at its own best learning rate, and the rate is
part of the protocol, not a tuning afterthought.** GeoTransolver's best rate
at the reporting protocol is 3e-3 on every DrivAerML rung and on the wings,
found by the two-rate control of rule 3; Transolver runs at 3e-3; ISLA runs
at 1e-3 at width 192 and at the width rule's starting rate above it
(@sec-using-lr). Why ISLA's rate does not simply follow the baselines' is a
property of the routing form and is explained once, in
@sec-isla-routing-forms.

## Datasets {#sec-datasets}

**Three datasets are training and evaluation sources, a fourth is a
zero-shot target, and four more, outside external aerodynamics, exercise
the parts of the interface the aerodynamic sets leave idle.** All supply
the same input schema, boundary cells with positions, outward normals and
measures plus the global conditions, so one model implementation runs on
all of them. Every aerodynamic one is an instance of external aerodynamics
with $K = 1$ global direction, the far-field flow direction, and
$S \in \{0, 1\}$ global scalars. This section says, per dataset, what the
problem is, what varies, what is predicted and what the model receives, at
the depth the results need; provenance, conversion, field names, sign
conventions, normalization, splits and pitfalls are in
@sec-datasets-detail.

| dataset | what it is | what varies | global inputs | role in the book |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **DrivAerML** (cars) | 484 parametrically morphed DrivAer notchback variants; time-averaged surface pressure and wall shear on the vehicle surface, plus volume fields | geometry only; one far-field condition | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | the Surface task: full-data accuracy, discretization and pose probes, capacity ladders; the Volume task: boundary to interior |
| **HiLiftAeroML** (wings) | 1,800 cases: 180 high-lift wing geometries (flap and slat settings by Latin hypercube), each at ten angles of attack from 4° to 22°; surface pressure, velocity and wall shear | geometry and far-field direction | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | data efficiency, unseen geometry, regime extrapolation |
| **AirfRANS** (airfoils) | 1,001 two-dimensional incompressible RANS solutions around NACA airfoils; pressure, velocity and turbulent viscosity in the volume | geometry, inlet direction and inlet speed | $K = 1$, $S = 1$ | the interior task on a second dataset; the training-case axis |
| **SHIFT-SUV** | sport-utility bodies in two rear-end families, estate and fastback; surface pressure and wall shear; same reference length and far-field direction as DrivAerML at a lower speed | geometry; a speed shift common to every architecture | $K = 1$, $S = 0$ | zero-shot transfer target only |

: The aerodynamic datasets. The four datasets beyond external aerodynamics are listed in @sec-datasets-beyond-aero. {#tbl-datasets-aero}

### DrivAerML: the Surface task and the Volume task {#sec-benchmarks}

**DrivAerML carries two tasks, named separately throughout the book because
they measure different things.** Geometry is the only variable, there is
one far-field condition, and every model is fed the vehicle surface alone:
the information diet of every published baseline on the dataset. The recipe
assigns 435 variants to training and 48 to validation, one validation set
shared by both tasks and every experiment. The reporting protocol samples
the recipe's default of 200,000 surface cells per case per step. The
**DrivAerML Surface task** predicts pressure and wall shear at those cells
(@sec-surface). The **DrivAerML Volume task** predicts pressure, velocity
and turbulent viscosity at 200,000 interior query points per car from the
surface alone (@sec-interior). A sentence that compares architectures on
DrivAerML names one of the two. @fig-problem-drivaer shows one validation
car with both tasks' fields (details: @sec-data-drivaer).

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-drivaer
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The DrivAerML problem, on one validation car. Top and middle: the
#|   vehicle surface (150,000 of its 17 million cells drawn at their
#|   centroids) colored by the time-averaged pressure coefficient
#|   $C_p = (p - p_\infty) / \tfrac{1}{2}\rho U_\infty^2$, the Surface task's
#|   scalar target, seen from the side and from above; the black arrow is the
#|   far-field flow direction, the one global vector input, and the far-field
#|   speed is the same for every car. Bottom: the symmetry plane of the volume
#|   mesh, colored by the speed ratio $|U| / U_\infty$, with the car's outline
#|   in black; the Volume task predicts pressure, velocity and turbulent
#|   viscosity at 200,000 query points drawn from this mesh, whose extent is
#|   printed. What varies per sample is the geometry only. What the model
#|   receives: the surface cells' positions, outward normals and areas, and the
#|   flow direction; the ground plane and the wind-tunnel boundaries are not
#|   inputs. How to read this: colors are the reference CFD
#|   fields, not predictions; the surface points are a random subset, so the
#|   density of dots is not the mesh resolution. Data:
#|   results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/drivaer.npz.
#| code-fold: true
D, Dm = load_problem("drivaer")
sp, cp = D["surf_points"], D["surf_cp"]
norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0.0, vmin=-1.5, vmax=1.0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8, 8.8), gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.0, 1.15, 1.35], hspace=0.4))
U = D["U_inf"]; bb = D["surf_bbox"]; x0 = bb[0, 0] - 1.9; z0 = 0.5 * (bb[0, 2] + bb[1, 2])
ax = axes[0]
depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 2]], sp[:, 1], cp, s=2.2, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm); map_axes(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("z [m]"); ax.set_title("side view: surface pressure coefficient $C_p$, the Surface task's scalar target", fontsize=9.5)
ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + 1.2, z0), xytext=(x0, z0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2.0))
ax.text(x0 + 0.6, z0 - 0.1, f"far field: uniform flow,\n$U_\\infty$ = {np.linalg.norm(U):.1f} m/s along $\\hat g_1$\n(the one global vector)", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=8.2, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlim(x0 - 0.2, bb[1, 0] + 0.3)
ax = axes[1]
sc = depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 1]], sp[:, 2], cp, s=2.2, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm); map_axes(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("y [m]"); ax.set_xlabel("x [m]"); ax.set_title("top view: $C_p$", fontsize=9.5); ax.set_xlim(x0 - 0.2, bb[1, 0] + 0.3)
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=axes[:2], fraction=0.025, pad=0.01, extend="min"); cb.set_label("$C_p$ [–]"); cb.outline.set_visible(False)
ax = axes[2]
q, um = D["slice_points"], D["slice_umag"]
sc2 = ax.scatter(q[:, 0], q[:, 2], c=um, s=1.8, lw=0, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=1.3, rasterized=True); map_axes(ax)
sil = sp[np.abs(sp[:, 1]) < 0.03]; ax.scatter(sil[:, 0], sil[:, 2], s=0.8, c=INK, lw=0, rasterized=True)
ax.set_ylabel("z [m]"); ax.set_xlabel("x [m]"); ax.set_title("symmetry plane $y = 0$ of the volume mesh: speed ratio $|U| / U_\\infty$ (the Volume task queries these points)", fontsize=9.5)
ib = D["interior_bbox"]
note(ax, f"volume mesh (query domain): {ib[0,0]:.0f} < x < {ib[1,0]:.0f} m, {ib[0,1]:.0f} < y < {ib[1,1]:.0f} m, {ib[0,2]:.1f} < z < {ib[1,2]:.0f} m\nground plane at z = {ib[0,2]:.2f} m (not an input)", loc="upper right")
cb2 = fig.colorbar(sc2, ax=[ax], fraction=0.025, pad=0.01, extend="max"); cb2.set_label("$|U| / U_\\infty$ [–]"); cb2.outline.set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

### HiLiftAeroML {#sec-dataset-hilift}

**HiLiftAeroML is a full geometry-by-angle grid, so it can hold out each
axis of variation on its own.** Every geometry appears at every angle, and
the dataset supports splits along three independent directions: how many
cases, which angles, and which geometries (@sec-splits). The model receives
the surface cells and the far-field direction $\hat g_1$, which carries the
angle of attack, and predicts pressure, temperature, density, velocity and
wall shear at those cells, at the same 200,000 cells per case as on the
cars. It is one of the two datasets on which the data-efficiency ladder is
measured (@sec-data-efficiency); the other is the DrivAerML Surface task.
@fig-problem-hilift shows one validation case (details: @sec-data-hilift).

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-hilift
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The HiLiftAeroML problem, on one validation case (a high-lift wing with
#|   slat and flap deployed, at 16° angle of attack). The wing surface
#|   (150,000 of its cells drawn at their centroids) colored by the pressure
#|   coefficient $C_p$, seen from above (top) and from the side (bottom); the
#|   black arrow is the far-field flow direction $\hat g_1$, the one global
#|   vector, which here carries the angle of attack. What varies per sample is
#|   the geometry (flap and slat settings) and the far-field direction (ten
#|   angles per geometry). What the model receives: surface cells with
#|   positions, outward normals and areas, and $\hat g_1$; it predicts
#|   pressure, temperature, density, velocity and wall shear on those cells.
#|   How to read this: the flow is compressible and the suction on the slat and
#|   the wing's leading edge runs far below the color scale's bottom, which is
#|   clipped; coordinates are converted from the dataset's inches to metres.
#|   Data: results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/hilift.npz.
#| code-fold: true
H, Hm = load_problem("hilift")
sp, cp = H["surf_points"], H["surf_cp"]
norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0.0, vmin=-4.0, vmax=1.0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 7.2), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[2.2, 1.0], hspace=0.08))
ax = axes[0]
sc = depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 1]], sp[:, 2], cp, s=2.2, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm); map_axes(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("y [m]"); ax.set_title(f"top view: $C_p$ on the upper surface; angle of attack {Hm['aoa_deg']:.0f}°", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]
depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 2]], -sp[:, 1], cp, s=2.2, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm); map_axes(ax)
U = H["U_inf"]; u = U / np.linalg.norm(U); bb = H["surf_bbox"]; Lc = 0.14 * (bb[1, 0] - bb[0, 0])
x0 = bb[0, 0] + 0.02 * (bb[1, 0] - bb[0, 0]); z0 = bb[1, 2] - 0.35 * (bb[1, 2] - bb[0, 2])
ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + Lc * u[0], z0 + Lc * u[2]), xytext=(x0, z0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2.0))
ax.text(x0 + 0.5 * Lc, z0 + 0.5 * Lc * u[2] + 0.12 * Lc, f"far field: uniform flow along $\\hat g_1$ at {Hm['aoa_deg']:.0f}°\n(Mach and Reynolds number fixed)", ha="left", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
ax.set_ylabel("z [m]"); ax.set_xlabel("x [m]"); ax.set_title("side view: $C_p$, the slat and the flap deflected below the wing", fontsize=9.5)
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=axes, fraction=0.02, pad=0.01, extend="min"); cb.set_label("$C_p$ [–]"); cb.outline.set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

### AirfRANS {#sec-dataset-airfrans}

**AirfRANS is the interior task on a second dataset and a second PDE
regime, and the first instance in the book of a global scalar input.** Its
full split trains on 800 airfoils and tests on 200. The boundary is the
airfoil polyline, about a thousand segments with in-plane normals and
segment lengths as the quadrature measure; the global inputs are the inlet
direction as the one global vector and the inlet speed as the one global
scalar; the interior queries, 100,000 per case, carry the signed distance to
the airfoil, and the model predicts pressure, velocity and turbulent
viscosity at them. The interior results are in @sec-interior-airfrans;
@fig-problem-airfrans shows one test case (details: @sec-data-airfrans).

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-airfrans
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The AirfRANS problem, on one test airfoil. Top: the boundary the model
#|   sees, the airfoil polyline of about a thousand segments with their
#|   outward normals (every twelfth drawn), the inlet direction $\hat g_1$
#|   (black arrow, the one global vector, at the angle of attack) and the inlet
#|   speed as the one global scalar; the interior queries carry the signed
#|   distance to the airfoil. Middle: the pressure coefficient
#|   $C_p = p / \tfrac{1}{2} U_\infty^2$ (kinematic pressure) at the interior
#|   mesh points in a window around the airfoil. Bottom: the speed ratio
#|   $|U| / U_\infty$ at the same points. What varies per sample is the
#|   airfoil shape, the inlet speed and its direction. What the model
#|   predicts: pressure, velocity and turbulent viscosity at the queries. How
#|   to read this: the queried domain extends well beyond this window (its
#|   extent is printed); the dots are 70,000 of the case's 179,000 mesh points
#|   and their density follows the mesh, fine near the wall and in the wake.
#|   Data: results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/airfrans.npz.
#| code-fold: true
A, Am = load_problem("airfrans")
bp, bc, bn = A["bnd_points"], A["bnd_cells"], A["bnd_normals"]; mid = bp[bc].mean(axis=1)
ip = A["int_points"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(8, 7.2), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.22))
ax = axes[0]
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(bp[bc][:, :, :2], colors=BC["free"], linewidths=2.0, zorder=3))
k = slice(None, None, 12); ax.quiver(mid[k, 0], mid[k, 1], bn[k, 0], bn[k, 1], color=MUTED, scale=28, width=0.0025, headwidth=3, zorder=2)
u = A["U_inf_dir"]; ax.annotate("", xy=(-0.45 + 0.3 * u[0], 0.38 + 0.3 * u[1]), xytext=(-0.45, 0.38), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2.0))
ax.text(-0.1, 0.40, f"inlet: uniform flow along $\\hat g_1$ at {Am['aoa_deg']:.2f}° (the global vector); $U_\\infty$ = {Am['U_inf_mag']:.1f} m/s (the global scalar); Re = {Am['Re']:.2g}", ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
ib = A["interior_bbox"]
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-0.5, 1.5); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.55); ax.set_ylabel("y / chord [–]")
ax.set_title(f"the boundary: {Am['n_boundary_cells']:,} line cells (position, normal, length), a no-slip wall; queries fill {ib[0,0]:.0f} < x < {ib[1,0]:.0f}, {ib[0,1]:.0f} < y < {ib[1,1]:.0f} chords", fontsize=9.2)
ax = axes[1]
sc = field_scatter(ax, ip[:, :2], A["int_cp"], s=2.5, signed=True, vmin=-1.0, vmax=1.0); map_axes(ax); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.55)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(bp[bc][:, :, :2], colors=INK, linewidths=0.8, zorder=3)); ax.set_ylabel("y / chord [–]")
ax.set_title("pressure coefficient $C_p$ at the interior points (target)", fontsize=9.5)
small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$C_p$ [–]", extend="both")
ax = axes[2]
sc = field_scatter(ax, ip[:, :2], A["int_umag"], s=2.5, vmin=0, vmax=1.3); map_axes(ax); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.55)
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(bp[bc][:, :, :2], colors=WHITE, linewidths=0.8, zorder=3)); ax.set_ylabel("y / chord [–]"); ax.set_xlabel("x / chord [–]")
ax.set_title("speed ratio $|U| / U_\\infty$ at the interior points (target)", fontsize=9.5)
small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$|U| / U_\\infty$ [–]", extend="max")
plt.show()
```

### SHIFT-SUV {#sec-shift-suv}

**No main result trains on SHIFT-SUV; its fastback family is the zero-shot
target.** The fastback family is held out from every model in the book and
is the zero-shot target of the cross-family transfer measurements
(@sec-scoreboard-200k); the estate family is a training source only where a
two-family model is compared. The model receives exactly what it receives
on DrivAerML. The lower far-field speed is a covariate shift identical for
every architecture, none of which receives the Reynolds number, and it is
reported alongside the geometry-family shift rather than corrected.
@fig-problem-shift-suv shows one fastback case (details:
@sec-data-shift-suv).

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-shift-suv
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The SHIFT-SUV zero-shot target, on one fastback case. The vehicle surface
#|   (150,000 of its 5 million cells at their centroids) colored by the
#|   pressure coefficient $C_p = (p - p_\infty) / \tfrac{1}{2}\rho U_\infty^2$,
#|   seen from the side and from above; the black arrow is the far-field
#|   direction $\hat g_1$. What varies per sample is the geometry; the far-field
#|   speed is fixed and lower than DrivAerML's, a covariate shift every model
#|   sees alike since none receives the Reynolds number. What the model
#|   receives is exactly what it receives on DrivAerML (positions, normals,
#|   areas, $\hat g_1$), which is what makes the zero-shot transfer possible.
#|   How to read this: the same color scale as @fig-problem-drivaer, so the
#|   two bodies can be compared by eye. Data:
#|   results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/shift_suv.npz.
#| code-fold: true
S_, Sm = load_problem("shift_suv")
sp, cp = S_["surf_points"], S_["surf_cp"]
norm = TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0.0, vmin=-1.5, vmax=1.0)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 5.6), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(height_ratios=[1.0, 1.15], hspace=0.15))
ax = axes[0]
depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 2]], sp[:, 1], cp, s=2.2, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm); map_axes(ax)
U = S_["U_inf"]; bb = S_["surf_bbox"]; x0 = bb[0, 0] - 1.9; z0 = 0.5 * (bb[0, 2] + bb[1, 2])
ax.annotate("", xy=(x0 + 1.2, z0), xytext=(x0, z0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2.0))
ax.text(x0 + 0.6, z0 - 0.1, f"far field: $U_\\infty$ = {np.linalg.norm(U):.0f} m/s\nalong $\\hat g_1$", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=8.2, color=INK2)
ax.set_xlim(x0 - 0.2, bb[1, 0] + 0.3)
ax.set_ylabel("z [m]"); ax.set_title(f"side view: $C_p$ on the {Sm['family']} family", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]
sc = depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 1]], sp[:, 2], cp, s=2.2, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=norm); map_axes(ax)
ax.set_ylabel("y [m]"); ax.set_xlabel("x [m]"); ax.set_title("top view: $C_p$", fontsize=9.5)
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=axes, fraction=0.025, pad=0.01, extend="min"); cb.set_label("$C_p$ [–]"); cb.outline.set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

### Datasets beyond external aerodynamics {#sec-datasets-beyond-aero}

**The architecture is written for any steady boundary-driven PDE, and
external aerodynamics is its benchmark instance, not its scope.** The next
benchmark instances are steady problems whose boundary conditions and loads
vary per sample, which exercise the global vector and scalar inputs and the
per-cell boundary scalars that the aerodynamic datasets leave at $K = 1$
and $n_b = 0$. Each is drawn below on one sample, with its boundary
conditions labeled where they act and one reference field beside them; the
model reads every mesh node as a query in all four:

- **PLAID Tensile2d** (@fig-problem-tensile2d; details:
  @sec-data-tensile2d): two-dimensional elasto-viscoplastic tension of a
  notched specimen; the top edge carries a pressure $P$ that varies per
  sample, the bottom edge is fixed, and five material parameters vary too.
  The model receives the outer polyline with per-cell labels (loaded,
  fixed, pinned) and the applied pressure as boundary scalars, $P$ and the
  material parameters as six global scalars, and the laboratory frame as
  two global vectors, because its targets are stress components in that
  frame (@sec-isla-heads); it predicts the three stress components, the
  cumulated plastic strain and the displacement.
- **GINOT Bracket Lug** (@fig-problem-lug; details: @sec-data-lug): a
  three-dimensional elastoplastic lug clamped at one end and pressed on the
  lower half of its hole; hole radius, length, thickness and pressure vary.
  The model receives the surface triangles with labels (fixed, hole,
  loaded) and the pressure as boundary scalars and the four design
  parameters as global scalars; it predicts the von Mises stress. Published
  Transolver and GNOT numbers exist for it.
- **OLBC** (@fig-problem-olbc-poisson, @fig-problem-olbc-elasticity;
  details: @sec-data-olbc): two sets on fixed meshes whose boundary is
  cut, per sample, into random segments carrying labeled Dirichlet, Neumann
  or Robin conditions with random values: a Poisson problem
  $-\nabla^2 u = f$ on a square with a random source (the $K = 0$ case,
  with the type and the value as per-cell boundary scalars) and
  plane-strain steel elasticity on a disc with two holes (per component a
  free segment, a prescribed displacement and two tractions; the laboratory
  frame as $K = 2$).

None of these carries a number in this book; the open axis they represent
is stated in @sec-limits-datasets, and the datasets scouted but not
adopted, with the conversion in progress, are in @sec-data-scouted.

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-tensile2d
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The PLAID Tensile2d problem, on one validation specimen. Left: the outer
#|   boundary, 496 line cells, colored by the condition each carries: the top
#|   edge is loaded by the pressure $P$ (a traction $-P\,n$; negative $P$ pulls),
#|   the bottom edge is fixed ($u_2 = 0$) with its left corner pinned
#|   ($u_1 = 0$, marked), and the curved notches are free; the box lists the
#|   six global scalars of this sample and the arrows the laboratory frame,
#|   the two global vectors. Middle: the axial stress $\sigma_{22}$ at the
#|   mesh nodes. Right: the displacement magnitude $|u|$. How to read this:
#|   the specimen's coordinates and stresses are in the dataset's units (a
#|   unit half-width; MPa-scale stresses); the nodes drawn are all 6,171 of
#|   this sample and every one is a query token; the loaded and fixed edges
#|   are where the per-cell boundary scalars are nonzero. Data:
#|   results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/tensile2d.npz.
#| code-fold: true
T, Tm = load_problem("tensile2d")
bp, bc = T["bnd_points"], T["bnd_cells"]; mid = bp[bc].mean(axis=1)
kinds = np.where(T["bc_loaded"] > 0.5, "flux", np.where(T["bc_fixed"] > 0.5, "value", "free"))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8, 4.2), sharey=True, gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.15, width_ratios=[1.75, 1, 1]))
ax = axes[0]
ax.scatter(T["int_points"][:, 0], T["int_points"][:, 1], s=1.2, c=GRID, lw=0, rasterized=True)
bc_segments(ax, bp, bc, kinds, lw=4.5)
pin = mid[T["bc_pinned"] > 0.5]; ax.plot(pin[:, 0], pin[:, 1], marker="^", ms=9, color=BC["value"], mec=INK, ls="none", zorder=5)
ax.text(0.0, 1.07, f"top edge: pressure P = {Tm['globals']['P']:.1f} (flux)", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8.5, color=BC["flux"], path_effects=halo())
ax.text(0.0, -1.08, "bottom edge: fixed $u_2$ = 0 (value)\ntriangle: pinned $u_1$ = 0", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=BC["value"], path_effects=halo())
ax.text(0.72, 0.0, "notches: free", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=BC["free"], rotation=90)
for v, lab in ((np.array([1, 0]), "$\\hat g_1$"), (np.array([0, 1]), "$\\hat g_2$")):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(-2.4 + 0.35 * v[0], -1.1 + 0.35 * v[1]), xytext=(-2.4, -1.1), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=1.6))
    ax.text(-2.4 + 0.5 * v[0], -1.1 + 0.5 * v[1], lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
g = Tm["globals"]
ax.text(-2.45, 1.0, "global scalars\n" + "\n".join(f"{k} = {g[k]:g}" for k in ("P", "p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "p5")), ha="left", va="top", fontsize=7.8, color=INK2,
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.3", fc="white", ec=BASELINE))
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.55, 1.3); ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 1.35); ax.set_ylabel("y [dataset units]"); ax.set_xlabel("x [dataset units]")
ax.set_title("conditions and global inputs", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]
sc = field_scatter(ax, T["int_points"][:, :2], T["sig22"], s=4.0, vmin=0, vmax=float(np.quantile(T["sig22"], 0.995))); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [dataset units]")
ax.set_title("axial stress $\\sigma_{22}$ (target)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$\\sigma_{22}$ [MPa]", extend="max")
ax = axes[2]
um = np.linalg.norm(T["displacement"], axis=1)
sc = field_scatter(ax, T["int_points"][:, :2], um * 1e3, s=4.0, vmin=0); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [dataset units]")
ax.set_title("displacement magnitude $|u|$ (target)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$|u|$ [$10^{-3}$ length units]")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-lug
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The GINOT Bracket Lug problem, on one test bracket. Left: the surface
#|   triangles that are the model's boundary tokens, colored by condition: the
#|   end face is clamped (value), the lower half of the hole carries the
#|   pressure (flux), the rest of the hole and the outer surface are free;
#|   orthographic view from above and in front (azimuth −60°, elevation 30°).
#|   Right: the von Mises stress at the mesh nodes projected along the hole's
#|   axis, the top face nearest; the box lists the four global scalars. What
#|   varies per sample: the hole radius, the length, the thickness and the
#|   pressure. How to read this: every node is a query token and the stress
#|   is the one target; the projection shows the top face's nodes over the
#|   interior ones, so the stress concentration at the hole is read on the
#|   surface. Data: results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/lug.npz.
#| code-fold: true
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d.art3d import Poly3DCollection
Lg, Lm = load_problem("lug")
bp, bc = Lg["bnd_points"] * 1e3, Lg["bnd_cells"]
kinds = np.where(Lg["bc_loaded"] > 0.5, "flux", np.where(Lg["bc_fixed"] > 0.5, "value", "free"))
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 3.6))
ax = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 1, projection="3d"); ax.set_proj_type("ortho")
tri = bp[bc]
face = np.array([BC[k] if k != "free" else "#d9d8d0" for k in kinds])
coll = Poly3DCollection(tri, facecolors=face, edgecolors="none", linewidths=0.1); ax.add_collection3d(coll)
ext = bp.max(0) - bp.min(0); c0 = 0.5 * (bp.max(0) + bp.min(0)); R = 0.5 * ext.max()
ax.set_xlim(bp[:, 0].min(), bp[:, 0].max()); ax.set_ylim(bp[:, 1].min(), bp[:, 1].max()); ax.set_zlim(bp[:, 2].min(), bp[:, 2].max()); ax.set_box_aspect(tuple(ext / ext.max()), zoom=1.0)
ax.view_init(elev=30, azim=-60); ax.set_axis_off()
ax.text2D(0.02, 0.90, "clamped end face: $u$ = 0 (value)", transform=ax.transAxes, color=BC["value"], fontsize=8.5, path_effects=halo())
ax.text2D(0.98, 0.14, "lower half of the hole:\npressure p (flux)", transform=ax.transAxes, color=BC["flux"], fontsize=8.5, ha="right", path_effects=halo())
ax.text2D(0.5, 0.02, "outer surface and upper hole: free", transform=ax.transAxes, color=BC["free"], fontsize=8.5, ha="center")
ax.set_title("boundary tokens and their conditions", fontsize=9.5, loc="left")
ax2 = fig.add_subplot(1, 2, 2)
ip = Lg["int_points"] * 1e3
sc = depth_scatter(ax2, ip[:, [0, 1]], ip[:, 2], Lg["von_mises"], s=6, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=float(np.quantile(Lg["von_mises"], 0.995))); map_axes(ax2)
g = Lm["globals"]
ax2.set_xlabel("x [mm]"); ax2.set_ylabel("y [mm]"); ax2.set_title("von Mises stress at the nodes (target)", fontsize=9.5)
small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax2, "von Mises [MPa]", extend="max")
fig.text(0.5, 0.0, f"this sample's global scalars: hole radius {1e3 * g['hole_radius']:.1f} mm, length {1e3 * g['length']:.1f} mm, thickness {1e3 * g['thickness']:.1f} mm, pressure {g['pressure_mpa']:.1f} MPa",
         ha="center", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2)
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-olbc-poisson
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The OLBC Poisson problem, $-\nabla^2 u = f$ on the square, on one test
#|   sample. Left: the boundary, 1,120 line cells, colored by the type of
#|   condition each segment carries in this sample (Dirichlet $u = g$, Neumann
#|   $\partial u / \partial n = g$, Robin $\alpha u + \partial u / \partial n = g$),
#|   with the prescribed value $g$ drawn as a curve offset from the edge (its
#|   scale in the corner). Middle: the source $f$, an input field given at the
#|   mesh nodes. Right: the solution $u$, the target. What varies per sample:
#|   where the segments are cut, which type each carries, the functions $g$
#|   and the source $f$; the mesh is the same for every sample. What the model
#|   receives: the boundary cells with positions, normals, lengths, a one-hot
#|   type and $g$ (and $\alpha$) as per-cell boundary scalars, no global
#|   vector, and every node as a query carrying $f$. How to read this: the
#|   Robin type appears in some samples and not others; this sample has none.
#|   Data: results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/olbc_poisson.npz.
#| code-fold: true
O, Om = load_problem("olbc_poisson")
bp, bc, bn = O["bnd_points"], O["bnd_cells"], O["bnd_normals"]; mid = bp[bc].mean(axis=1)
kinds = np.where(O["bc_dirichlet"] > 0.5, "value", np.where(O["bc_neumann"] > 0.5, "flux", np.where(O["bc_robin"] > 0.5, "robin", "free")))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8, 3.7), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.3))
ax = axes[0]
bc_segments(ax, bp, bc, kinds, lw=4.0)
gscale = 0.12 / max(1e-9, float(np.abs(O["bc_value_g"]).max()))
off = mid[:, :2] + bn[:, :2] * (0.06 + gscale * O["bc_value_g"][:, None])
for k in ("value", "flux", "robin"):
    m = kinds == k
    if m.any():
        ax.scatter(off[m, 0], off[m, 1], s=2.5, c=BC[k], lw=0, rasterized=True)
ax.plot([1.08, 1.08], [-1.0, -1.0 + 0.12], color=INK2, lw=1.0); ax.text(1.12, -0.94, f"g = {float(np.abs(O['bc_value_g']).max()):.1f}", fontsize=7.5, color=INK2, va="center")
present = [k for k in ("value", "flux", "robin") if (kinds == k).any()]
bc_legend(ax, present, loc="lower center")
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-1.4, 1.4); ax.set_ylim(-2.05, 1.3); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]"); ax.set_ylabel("y [–]")
ax.set_title("conditions: type, and value $g$", fontsize=9.5)
ax = axes[1]
sc = field_scatter(ax, O["int_points"][:, :2], O["source"], s=2.5, signed=True); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]")
ax.set_title("source $f$ (input at the nodes)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$f$ [–]")
ax = axes[2]
sc = field_scatter(ax, O["int_points"][:, :2], O["u"], s=2.5, signed=True); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]")
ax.set_title("solution $u$ (target)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$u$ [–]")
for ax in axes[1:]:
    ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.05); ax.set_yticklabels([])
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-problem-olbc-elasticity
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The OLBC elasticity problem, plane-strain steel on a disc with two holes,
#|   on one test sample. Left: the three boundary loops; on the outer circle
#|   each of the two displacement components has its own condition, drawn as
#|   two concentric rings (outer ring: the $x$ component; inner ring: the $y$
#|   component), a prescribed displacement (value), a traction (flux) or free;
#|   the smaller hole is clamped in both components, the larger is free. The
#|   arrows are the laboratory frame, the two global vectors. Middle: the von
#|   Mises stress from the three stress components at the nodes. Right: the
#|   displacement magnitude. What varies per sample: where the outer circle is
#|   cut, which condition each segment and component carries, and the values.
#|   What the model receives: the loops' cells with normals, lengths, the
#|   per-component one-hot type and the prescribed displacement and traction
#|   components as boundary scalars, the frame, and every node as a query; it
#|   predicts the three stress components and the displacement. How to read
#|   this: all quantities are in the dataset's dimensionless units (stress per
#|   100 MPa, length per metre). Data:
#|   results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/olbc_elasticity.npz.
#| code-fold: true
E, Em = load_problem("olbc_elasticity")
bp, bc, bn = E["bnd_points"], E["bnd_cells"], E["bnd_normals"]; mid = bp[bc].mean(axis=1)
def kinds_of(comp):
    return np.where(E[f"bc_dirichlet_{comp}"] > 0.5, "value", np.where(E[f"bc_neumann_{comp}"] > 0.5, "flux", "free"))
kx, ky = kinds_of("x"), kinds_of("y")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(8, 3.9), gridspec_kw=dict(wspace=0.3))
ax = axes[0]
outer = E["loop_id"] < 0.5
segs = bp[bc][:, :, :2]
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs[outer] + 0.045 * bn[outer, None, :2], colors=[BC[k] for k in kx[outer]], linewidths=4.0, capstyle="butt"))
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs[outer] - 0.0 * bn[outer, None, :2], colors=[BC[k] for k in ky[outer]], linewidths=4.0, capstyle="butt"))
ax.add_collection(LineCollection(segs[~outer], colors=[BC[k] for k in kx[~outer]], linewidths=4.0, capstyle="butt"))
ax.scatter(E["int_points"][:, 0], E["int_points"][:, 1], s=0.8, c=GRID, lw=0, rasterized=True, zorder=0)
for v, lab in ((np.array([1, 0]), "$\\hat g_1$"), (np.array([0, 1]), "$\\hat g_2$")):
    ax.annotate("", xy=(1.05 + 0.3 * v[0], 0.8 + 0.3 * v[1]), xytext=(1.05, 0.8), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=1.6))
    ax.text(1.05 + 0.46 * v[0], 0.8 + 0.46 * v[1], lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
bc_legend(ax, ["value", "flux", "free"], loc="lower center")
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-1.55, 1.6); ax.set_ylim(-2.15, 1.3); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]"); ax.set_ylabel("y [–]")
ax.set_title("conditions, per component\nouter ring: on $u_x$; inner ring: on $u_y$", fontsize=9.0)
vm = np.sqrt(E["sig11"] ** 2 - E["sig11"] * E["sig22"] + E["sig22"] ** 2 + 3 * E["sig12"] ** 2)
ax = axes[1]
sc = field_scatter(ax, E["int_points"][:, :2], vm, s=2.5, vmin=0, vmax=float(np.quantile(vm, 0.995))); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]")
ax.set_title("von Mises stress (from targets)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$\\sigma_\\mathrm{vM}$ [–]", extend="max")
ax = axes[2]
um = np.linalg.norm(E["displacement"], axis=1)
sc = field_scatter(ax, E["int_points"][:, :2], um * 1e4, s=2.5, vmin=0); map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [–]")
ax.set_title("displacement $|u|$ (target)", fontsize=9.5); small_colorbar(fig, sc, ax, "$|u|$ [$10^{-4}$]")
for ax in axes[1:]:
    ax.set_ylim(-1.05, 1.05); ax.set_yticklabels([])
plt.show()
```

**Splits.** Every split in the book is either the dataset's curated
manifest used unchanged or a fixed-seed permutation recorded in the
manifest; the HiLiftAeroML split table, which holds out one question per
split, and the other datasets' splits are in @sec-splits. Two facts bear on
reading the results: DrivAerML has one validation set of 48 cars, shared by
the Surface and Volume tasks and by every experiment, with a training set
of 435 cars or a nested rung of 27, 54, 109 or 218 (@sec-data-efficiency);
and the HiLiftAeroML test manifests overlap, so a test split is sealed per
checkpoint, not per program (@sec-limits-validation).

## Protocol {#sec-protocol}

**One frozen recipe produces every cross-architecture number in the book;
a comparison that departs from it says so in the same sentence.**

| item | setting |
|---|---|
| cells per case | 200,000 sampled surface cells per case per step, the recipe default and the reporting protocol, every architecture and every dataset; on the interior tasks, 200,000 interior queries per case on DrivAerML and 100,000 on AirfRANS |
| exploration budget | 10,000 cells per case: appears only as a labeled rung of a cell-count ladder or as the labeled setting of a mechanism control, never as an accuracy standing |
| epochs and schedule | 500 epochs, one case per step; the learning rate is divided by ten every 100 epochs, so the effective budget is about 300 epochs at a useful rate |
| arithmetic | bfloat16 autocast in training; float32 at evaluation (@sec-metrics) |
| augmentation | none |
| learning rate | each architecture at its own best rate at the reporting protocol: ISLA $10^{-3}$ at width 192 and the width rule's rate above it (@sec-using-lr), GeoTransolver and Transolver $3 \times 10^{-3}$; every row names the rate it uses (@sec-lr-protocol) |
| global inputs | each global direction as a unit vector, each magnitude as a scalar, for every architecture (@sec-unit-direction-rule) |
| seeds | two or more (42 and 43 unless stated), reported individually beside the mean |
| checkpoint | the final epoch; no selection on validation error |
| datasets | a result counts when it is reproduced on two datasets; a single-dataset result is labeled as such |
| validation and test | all architectures at all rungs scored on the same validation cases; a sealed test split is evaluated exactly once with the checkpoint and configuration declared in writing beforehand |
| preregistration | every experiment states its prediction and its falsifier in readout units before it runs; the dated record is the notebook (@sec-notebook) |

Because the rungs of a ladder share one rate and one schedule, a difference
between rungs is a difference in data and nothing else. When a result
favors one architecture, the strongest controls for the other (a higher
learning rate, doubled epochs, a same-family architecture without the
geometry encoder) run under the same recipe before the result is stated.

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="What the validation set is used for"}
The HiLiftAeroML and DrivAerML accuracy figures in this book are
validation-set figures with no checkpoint selection behind them, and with
this much adaptive reuse disclosed: the per-architecture learning rate is
chosen on the full split by validation; Transolver's rate is chosen per
small-data rung on it; the ablations that follow earlier readouts are
designed after reading it; and the choice of which results to present is
made with it in view. The HiLiftAeroML test splits are spent only on the
regime-extrapolation evaluations and one diagnostic run alongside them (a
variant of ISLA given raw coordinates), and because those test sets cover
every geometry (@sec-splits), the remaining test manifests are held out per
checkpoint but are not program-level confirmations (@sec-limits-validation).
:::

Every figure and table caption ends with the artifact in `results/` from
which it is computed, and every figure is drawn from that artifact at render
time.
